analysis.one_liner: Delays the phaseout of the ozone-depleting fumigant methyl bromide by ten years.
analysis.headline: The bill never left a House subcommittee and died when the 106th Congress ended in January 2001.
analysis.plain_summary: Methyl bromide is a pesticide used to fumigate crops, stored grain, and food facilities, but it damages the ozone layer and US law scheduled it for elimination in 2005. This bill would have pushed that date back to 2015, matching the slower schedule the international Montreal Protocol gives developing countries, and would have permanently exempted fumigation done for pest and sanitation rules. It was referred to the House Commerce Committee, sent to its Health and Environment Subcommittee, and never received a vote.
analysis.who_benefits: If it had passed, growers and food handlers who rely on methyl bromide — strawberry, tomato, and nursery operators, grain storage facilities, and the companies that make and import the chemical — would have kept using it for ten more years without facing the stricter US phaseout schedule.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Fumigant makers and growers who use it

how_it_helps.text: Delays the deadline for ending US production of methyl bromide from January 1, 2005 to January 1, 2015, and requires EPA to follow a phaseout no stricter than the schedule the Montreal Protocol sets for developing countries [S2][S3].

Exempts from the phaseout any methyl bromide used to fumigate commodities, articles, or storage and processing facilities to meet Animal and Plant Health Inspection Service requirements or any sanitation or food protection standard [S2][S3].

analysis.who_pays: Ordinary people would bear the cost through a slower repair of the ozone layer and continued exposure to a toxic fumigant, particularly for people living and working near treated fields and storage facilities.
analysis.who_pays_short: People near treated fields and the ozone layer

drawbacks.text: Methyl bromide depletes the stratospheric ozone layer, which is why the Clean Air Act and the Montreal Protocol scheduled it for elimination; delaying that by a decade slows the layer's recovery [S2].

Supporters argued that growers had no affordable substitutes for quarantine and pre-plant fumigation, and that losing methyl bromide on the 2005 timetable while trading partners still used it would raise food costs and put US produce at a disadvantage — the burden honest backers would have had to acknowledge [S2][S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit was a cheaper, more reliable pest-control tool for a specific set of growers and food handlers for ten more years. The cost was a decade of added ozone depletion and toxic-fumigant exposure spread across the public. The bill never received a vote, so lawmakers never had to weigh that trade-off on the record.

outcome.mechanism: It was sent to the House Commerce Committee and then to its Health and Environment Subcommittee in April 2000, where it sat without a hearing or vote until the Congress ended in January 2001 [S1][S5].

narrative.text: Rep. Richard Pombo introduced the bill on April 6, 2000, with three original cosponsors, and 57 members total signed on — 47 Republicans, 9 Democrats, and 1 Independent [S4].
The House referred it to the Committee on Commerce the day it was introduced [S5].
On April 24, 2000 it was referred to the Subcommittee on Health and Environment, and no further action was taken for the rest of the Congress [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: The public came out ahead: the 2005 phaseout of an ozone-depleting toxic fumigant stayed on the books because the bill never moved. Manufacturers, importers, and heavy agricultural users of methyl bromide would have been the beneficiaries had it passed.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: The public; growers kept a stalled delay

for.name: Rep. Richard W. Pombo
for.what_they_did: Sponsored the bill to delay the methyl bromide phaseout to 2015 and exempt sanitation fumigation [S1][S3]

for.name: Reps. Miller of Florida, Thurman, and Aderholt
for.what_they_did: Joined Pombo in introducing the bill on April 6, 2000 [S3][S4]

for.name: 47 of 57 cosponsors
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill, giving it a broad Republican bloc of support [S4]

against.name: Rep. Michael Bilirakis
against.role: Chair, House Commerce Subcommittee on Health and Environment
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled a hearing or markup on the bill after it was referred to his subcommittee on April 24, 2000 [S5]

against.name: Rep. Tom Bliley
against.what_they_did: Never brought the bill before the full committee or to the House floor during the remainder of the 106th Congress [S5]

sides.party_line_note: No vote was ever held, so the outcome never split by party; the 57 cosponsors were bipartisan but skewed Republican (47 R, 9 D, 1 I) [S4].

industries.industry: Agricultural producers and food handlers using methyl bromide
industries.note: The bill would have let growers of strawberries, tomatoes, nursery stock, and grain storage operators keep using the fumigant for quarantine and sanitation until 2015 instead of 2005. Their cheaper pest control would come at the cost of ozone depletion and toxic exposure for nearby communities and farmworkers.
A ten-year delay in the phaseout, plus a broad exemption for fumigation done to meet pest and sanitation rules, would have preserved the companies' market for a chemical scheduled to be eliminated.
